clinicalPearls: Presents in the first months of life, earlier than classic Rett syndrome, with severe developmental impairment and absent early milestones rather than a regression after normal early development
Postnatal (acquired) microcephaly with deceleration of head growth is characteristic
A prominent dyskinetic movement disorder with stereotypies, chorea, dystonia and hand automatisms is a hallmark feature
Feeding difficulties, gastro-oesophageal reflux, irritability and disordered sleep are common in infancy
Epilepsy is frequent, and brain imaging often shows a thin or hypoplastic corpus callosum, simplified gyration and delayed myelination
Caused by loss-of-function of FOXG1, a forkhead-box transcription factor essential to early forebrain (telencephalic) development, usually as a de novo autosomal dominant variant or a 14q12 deletion
Unlike classic Rett syndrome (MECP2), FOXG1 syndrome affects both sexes and lacks the typical period of normal early development
reference.pathophysiology: FOXG1 encodes a forkhead-box transcription factor that is a master regulator of early forebrain patterning, controlling telencephalic progenitor proliferation, cortical neuron layering and corpus callosum formation. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants or 14q12 deletions reduce functional protein, disrupting the developmental programme that builds the cerebral cortex and interhemispheric connections. The resulting structural and connectivity abnormalities produce the profound congenital encephalopathy, movement disorder and acquired microcephaly. Because the primary defect is in prenatal brain construction rather than in later synaptic maintenance, the phenotype is congenital rather than regressive.
additionalDifferentials: Other early-infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to assess corpus callosum, gyration, myelination and frontal lobe volume
EEG to characterise epileptiform activity and background
Chromosomal microarray to detect 14q12 deletions or duplications
Targeted FOXG1 sequencing or a Rett/epileptic-encephalopathy gene panel or exome sequencing
redFlags: Rapidly decelerating head circumference indicating acquired microcephaly
Feeding failure, aspiration or faltering growth
Severe irritability or sleep disruption affecting the child and family
reference.prognosis: FOXG1 syndrome is a severe lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder with profound intellectual disability, absent speech and limited independent mobility. Life expectancy can be reduced by seizures and respiratory or feeding complications, and care is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Labelling the child as having cerebral palsy and not pursuing a genetic diagnosis
Assuming Rett syndrome requires a female patient and a regression history, thereby missing the congenital FOXG1 variant
Overlooking the dyskinetic movement disorder or misattributing it solely to seizures
Failing to recognise that FOXG1 duplications cause a distinct, epilepsy-predominant phenotype different from deletions
